title: At home
text: mom is home. dad is here. we have tea. the sun is up. a cup is on the desk. mom has a book. dad has a map. we sit and talk. the room is warm. a bird is by the window. we have a nice day at home.

title: Our cat
text: we have a cat. the cat sleeps by the door. in the morning it asks for food. our cat likes a soft rug. it plays with a ball in the day. then it goes to its bowl. when the bowl is empty, the cat makes a small sound. we give it food and clean water. after a meal, it goes back to sleep. at night, it waits for us by the door.

title: A sunny day
text: the sun is warm. we go to the park. the trees are tall and the birds sing. it is a good day. we take some water and walk on a small path. a duck swims in the pond. dry leaves lie on the grass. my friend finds a smooth stone and shows it to me. we sit on a bench and look at the sky. we plan to be home before the evening comes.

title: A cup of tea
text: in the morning i put a cup on the table. a book is near it. the tea is ready, and i can read in peace. the sky is bright. I turn a page and read about a town far away. Fresh bread smells good in the kitchen. A green plant stands by the window, where I watered it yesterday. No one is in a hurry, so I can finish the whole chapter. Later, I close the book and tell my family about the part I liked most.

title: The way home
text: after a walk we go home along a quiet street. our dog waits by the gate. it wags its tail because it is happy to see us. soon we will have dinner. On the way, we meet a neighbor with a bicycle and wish him a good evening. The sky turns pink, and the streetlights begin to shine. At home, I take off my coat, wash my hands, and help set the table. During dinner, everyone shares a story from the day. Even a simple walk can leave a happy memory.

title: Morning in town
text: Early in the morning, the town wakes up. People wait for the bus, and a bakery smells of fresh bread. I check the time and decide to walk. It feels like a quiet start to the day. Small shops open around the square, and a cleaner sweeps fallen leaves near the fountain. At the corner, a car stops to let people cross the road. I see a familiar baker and say hello. He smiles and wishes me a good day. As I keep walking, the town grows louder: footsteps, conversations, and bicycle bells fill the air.

title: A small garden
text: My grandmother has a small garden behind her house. In spring, we plant flowers and water the soil. Each day we look for new leaves. When the first flower opens, everyone smiles and wants to see it. One morning, after a cold night, we noticed that the soil had become dry. Grandma explained why plants need water, but why too much water can also hurt them. We gently loosened the soil and removed a few weeds. By the end of summer, the garden was full of color, and butterflies visited the flowers. Each plant seemed to have its own little story.

title: A visit to the library
text: On Saturday, we visited the library. I wanted a book about the sea, while my sister looked for stories about animals. The librarian showed us the right shelf. We chose two books and walked home to read. The reading room was bright and quiet. I heard only the soft sound of turning pages. I found a map of islands and compared its names with the pictures in my book. My sister learned new facts about foxes and owls. Before leaving, we wrote down the return dates so we would not forget them. On the way home, we shared our favorite discoveries.

title: A new recipe
text: Today we decided to bake cookies. First we measured flour, butter, and sugar, then mixed everything in a bowl. While the dough rested, I cleared the table. Soon a sweet smell filled the kitchen and made us hungry. While the cookies baked, we set out plates and made some tea. I wanted to open the oven early, but my sister reminded me to wait until the dough turned golden. When the timer rang, we carefully took out the tray and let the cookies cool. The first bite was crisp and sweet. Next time, we plan to add a little cinnamon.

title: An evening by the lake
text: When evening came, we walked to the lake. The water was calm, and small lights appeared across the shore. My friend suggested that we stay a little longer to watch the first stars. We sat quietly and listened to the wind in the grass. A narrow path of moonlight appeared across the water. Someone laughed quietly nearby, and birds moved through the reeds. We remembered a funny moment from our summer trip and promised to meet more often. When the air grew cold, I zipped up my jacket. On the way home, we talked about a new place to visit next summer.

title: An unexpected question
text: Why do leaves change color in autumn? I wondered about this during a walk. At home, I opened a book and learned about the green pigment called chlorophyll. Even familiar trees, it turns out, can hold surprising secrets! The next day, I asked my teacher, "Why do some leaves turn yellow earlier than others?" She suggested watching the weather and the hours of sunlight. We wrote our observations in a notebook and compared the trees near our school. We did not find every answer at once, but looking for them was more exciting than reading a finished explanation. Now I notice more on every walk.

title: A kind gesture
text: On my way to the store, I saw a neighbor carrying heavy bags. "Would you like some help?" I asked. She smiled and handed me one of them. We walked to her door, talked about the weather, and wished each other a pleasant day. At her door, my neighbor said, "Thank you! Without your help, I would still be carrying those bags." I told her it was no trouble at all. We met again the next day, and she offered me an apple from her garden. I thanked her but said I did not need a gift. Sometimes a brief conversation can make a familiar street feel more friendly.

title: Weekend plans
text: On Friday, my friends discussed their weekend plans. One wanted to visit a museum, while another hoped for a bike ride. We checked the forecast and asked, "Will it rain in the morning?" If the weather is good, we will go to the park first and visit an exhibition later. "What if the museum is closed?" Max asked. We agreed to check its opening hours and make a backup plan. Then we shared small tasks: Lena would bring water, I would check the tickets, and Dan would carry a map. By evening, our plan was ready. Everyone understood that a good weekend depends less on a strict schedule than on pleasant company.

title: A small discovery
text: An old globe stood in the classroom. Our teacher asked us to find a place we had never visited. I chose a small island and began reading about its wildlife. I learned that unusual trees grow there, and some birds cannot be found anywhere else in the world. Later, I found photos of the island and showed them to my friends. In one picture, the sea was bright blue; in another, dark rocks rose above the waves. We discussed how animals adapt to life far from large continents. "It must be very quiet there," a friend said. I hoped to visit the island one day, but for now I was happy to travel through maps, stories, and books.

title: A letter to a friend
text: Dear friend, today I visited the mountains for the first time! At first, the path seemed easy, but soon the climb became steep. A cool wind greeted us at the top, and I forgot how tired I was. I took a few photos and wrote down what I saw, hoping to remember this day for years. That evening, we stayed in a small house at the foot of the mountain. The owner told us how quickly the weather changes at high altitude and advised us to carry warm clothes. I sat by the window for a long time, watching clouds hide the distant peaks. If we go there again, I will bring a notebook; so many thoughts appear during a journey and disappear before we return home. I hope we can make such a trip together someday!

title: A cooking lesson
text: For our vegetable soup, we used 3 potatoes, 2 carrots, and 1 onion. We washed the vegetables, cut them into small pieces, and placed a pot on the stove. After 20 minutes, the soup was ready. The cook had one rule: prepare the ingredients before turning on the heat. While the water warmed, we placed 4 plates on the table and cut 200 grams of bread. I copied the recipe so we could use it at home: add vegetables one by one, season the soup near the end, and let it stand for 5 minutes. With 2 liters of water, there was enough for our family. After lunch, we discussed what to change if we needed to serve 6 people instead of 4.

title: The early train
text: Our train left at 6:40, so the alarm rang at 5:15. At the station, we found platform 4 and checked the car number. Inside, everything was quiet: some passengers read, while others watched the view or slept. After 30 minutes, fields appeared outside the window in the morning light. We asked the conductor about our arrival time: 9:25. It turned out that the next part of the journey would take nearly 50 minutes. I opened my book but soon looked out the window again. Small villages passed by, and mist hung over the river. At 8:10, we visited the dining car for tea. When we returned, I checked our tickets and wrote down a few impressions to share with friends later.

title: A walking route
text: We planned a 5-kilometer walk: from home to the park, then to the bridge and back. The map showed 3 places to rest. Along the way, we found a small cafe next to a tall tree. My friends wanted to stop, but I reminded them that sunset was only 40 minutes away. We walked the first 1.5 kilometers in 20 minutes, a little faster than planned. In the park, we met a family with a dog and showed them the way to the pond. At a crossroads, a sign said the bridge was 800 meters away. We took several photos and then turned back. The final route was better than our old one: fewer busy roads and more shady paths. We hope to repeat the walk in 2 weeks.

title: A night of stars
text: In the evening, we watched the stars. A phone screen said, "You may see 5 bright planets tonight." We managed to find 2, but the clouds hid the rest. My younger sister asked why stars did not fall to Earth. I explained that distances in space are much greater than they appear. I opened a sky map and tried to find a group of stars I had seen the week before. The app suggested an observation time of 21:30 and warned us about light clouds. We decided to go outside in 15 minutes. At first, we noticed an airplane instead of a planet, then a satellite moving slowly between the stars. My sister wrote down three questions for her school project, and I promised to help her find the answers.

title: First steps in code
text: In class, we built a small program. It asked, "What is 7 + 8?" The user typed an answer, and the program checked it. At first, I entered 16, but then I found the mistake and fixed the calculation. Our teacher said that finding errors is just as important as writing code that works. We added two more examples: 12 - 5 and 6 * 3. The program had to check an answer and explain a mistake in simple words. I wrote a few tests and noticed that an empty line caused an exception. After a small fix, the program asked the user to try again instead of closing. At the end of class, we agreed on a useful rule: check that the input is valid before doing the calculation.

title: A note on the desk
text: Before leaving home, I wrote a note: "Back after 18:00. Dinner is in the fridge." My plans changed, however, because the bus was delayed by road work. I sent a message so no one would worry. When I finally arrived, everyone smiled and asked about my day; I told them about a surprising meeting on the way. At the bus stop, the display showed a 12-minute delay, but the expected time changed again. I decided to walk to the next stop and entered a little bookshop along the way. The owner recommended a collection of travel stories. "Remember to check the schedule tonight," he said. When I finally reached home, it was already 18:35. Still, I had a new book in my bag, and I felt better than I had in the morning.

title: The idea workshop
text: Our club decided to build a model bridge. First we gathered supplies: cardboard, a ruler, glue, and 12 wooden sticks. One person drew a plan, another checked the measurements, and I helped with assembly. When the bridge began to tilt, we did not argue; instead, we tested a few ideas and strengthened its base. To compare our designs, we tested each bridge with a 250-gram weight placed in the middle. The first model bent, the second carried the weight, and the third was too heavy. We drew a new plan at a scale of 1:10 and marked the pieces we could remove without making the structure weaker. After three attempts, the bridge finally stood firmly. Our club leader praised not just the finished model, but the fact that we had tested every claim.

title: Rain at night
text: Heavy rain began during the night, but by morning the sky was clear. Puddles on the sidewalk reflected houses and streetlights. I went out for bread and noticed a sign on the bakery door: "We open at 8:30." There were still 10 minutes to wait, so I walked along the river, listened to the birds, and returned just in time. The riverbank looked different after the rain: drops hung from the metal rails, and wet branches reflected the soft morning light. Near a bench, I found a forgotten umbrella and took it to a nearby kiosk. The seller promised to return it if the owner came looking. At 8:29, I walked back to the bakery. Through the window, I saw fresh rolls on the shelves and steam rising from warm bread. A short wait had unexpectedly turned into a pleasant walk.

title: A museum of old things
text: At a museum, I saw objects used about 100 years ago: a clock with a pendulum, an early telephone, and a typewriter. The guide explained how each invention answered a need of its time. I spent the longest time looking at the typewriter keys. They required a firm touch, yet every press left a clear letter on the page. In the next room, we saw photographs of old workshops: long desks, ink ribbons, and metal parts. Our guide asked us to compare the typewriter with a modern keyboard. Both have keys, but they feel very different under the fingers. A label gave the year of manufacture as 1924. I imagined how many letters and notes people had typed on that machine over the decades. Before leaving, we stopped to read about the mechanic who had kept it working.

title: An unexpected discovery
text: While sorting old boxes, we found a notebook filled with stories. The first page said, "Ideas come to people who ask questions." Inside were travel notes, sketches of houses, and a summer reading list. I read a few pages and realized that ordinary memories become more vivid when we notice small details: weather, conversations, and unexpected meetings. On the last page, the writer had left a question: "What would you like to remember in 10 years?" I decided to start a notebook of my own. On the first day, I wrote about my walk to school, a talk with a friend, and the smell of wet grass. The next day, I recorded a surprising story told by an elderly neighbor. Slowly, I realized that the value of a diary lies not in its length but in careful attention. Sometimes one precise word brings back a memory better than a long description. I try to write simply and notice more.

title: The city wakes up
text: At 7:10, I stepped outside and noticed how quickly the city changes in the morning. A small line formed near the subway, a bus driver greeted passengers, and a bookseller arranged new titles in the window. Somewhere nearby, a person played a guitar; the soft melody mixed with traffic. I wrote down three things I had noticed because I wanted to turn them into a story. By evening, those small details helped me remember the whole day. At a crossing, I heard a street musician say to a passerby, "The city sounds different today." I liked that thought and began to listen to its rhythm: a short tram bell, wheels on wet stones, a quiet talk between two students. At a corner cafe, the barista wrote number 17 on my order while another customer discussed an art exhibition. On my way back, I realized that a good story does not always need an extraordinary event. Sometimes it begins with a familiar street, a few exact details, and a connection between them.

title: A walk to the lighthouse
text: We walked toward an old lighthouse at the edge of a bay. The route was longer than it looked on the map: first we climbed a stone staircase, then crossed a grove of tall trees. Along the way, I counted 6 benches and 2 signs, but not a single shop. When we finally saw the tower, the fog began to lift. A guide explained that the lighthouse once helped ships find a safe route home. Looking across the water, I wondered how much could depend on one reliable signal. A faded photograph of the bay, taken in 1968, hung on the lookout wall. We compared it with the view outside: the coast had changed little, but houses now stood where old warehouses had been. The guide invited us to climb upstairs to see a small island. The stairs took 12 minutes, and the last steps were difficult. At the top, we watched a fishing boat pass between two rocky points. The wind grew stronger, so we did not stay near the window for long. Walking back, we discussed simple inventions that had once made travel safer: maps, compasses, clocks, and warning lights.

title: A backyard experiment
text: One afternoon, we decided to test which surface warmed up fastest in the sun. We filled 3 identical cups with water and placed them on wood, stone, and metal. Every 15 minutes, we noted the temperature and tried not to miss a reading. By evening, the result surprised us: the cup on dark metal had warmed the most. We repeated the test the next day to see whether a passing breeze had affected the result. A simple question had slowly become a real experiment. We entered the measurements into a table and noticed that our results might reflect more than the material beneath each cup. For example, one cup stood closer to a wall and spent part of the afternoon in the shade. We moved the cups to equal distances and repeated our readings at 12:00, 12:15, and 12:30. Then we compared the averages, discussed possible mistakes, and wrote a careful conclusion. An honest experiment takes patience: getting a number is not enough; we must check what it means. Our teacher suggested a third test with a different amount of water.

title: A conversation about the future
text: At our club meeting, everyone shared a skill they hoped to learn this year. Lena wanted to speak a new language, Alex planned to study photography, and I hoped to type quickly without looking at the keyboard. We agreed on a simple plan: practice a little each day, record our progress, and avoid comparing our first attempts with someone else's experience. "Even 10 minutes a day can matter," one friend said. A month later, we met again and discovered how much steady effort had changed our habits. After a few weeks, we learned that our plans fitted everyday life in different ways. One person practiced before breakfast, another found time only at night, and a third preferred several short sessions of 5 minutes. We compared notes but refused to name a single winner: everyone had a different pace. At our next meeting, we decided to record not only speed but also the strength of the habit. "You cannot expect the same result every day," Lena said. What matters is understanding why today felt easier or harder and calmly returning to practice tomorrow.

title: A story about practice
text: When I first tried to learn touch typing, my fingers searched for every key. I believed that speed mattered more than anything else, so I rushed and overlooked mistakes. Later, I changed my approach: I focused on accuracy first and raised my pace little by little. Each evening, I completed one lesson, reviewed the results, and noticed what had improved since the day before. Some days the progress was barely visible; after 30 days, however, I felt much more confident with a keyboard. I learned that a useful habit rarely grows from one heroic effort. It grows from many small efforts, repeated with patience and care. One day, I decided to look not only at my final speed but also at what I did while typing. I noticed that I made more mistakes when I watched the timer instead of the next character. I turned off unnecessary hints, chose a short text, and focused on an even rhythm. After a week, I made fewer mistakes, although my speed did not improve immediately. Later, I tried a harder mode: long passages required more attention, while familiar words helped me stay steady. I learned that a good typing trainer should show progress without making every mistake feel like a punishment. If I press the wrong key, I can simply try again and move on. A few months later, practice no longer felt like a test. It had become a quiet habit that helped me write letters, take notes, and work on my own ideas. That calm consistency was the most valuable result of all.
